interactions.label: A hordeolum internum differs from a hordeolum externum primarily because it:

params.question: A hordeolum internum differs from a hordeolum externum primarily because it:

answers.text: Is caused by a different organism than Staphylococcus aureus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both hordeolum externum and internum are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. The difference lies in which gland is infected, not the causative organism.

answers.text: Involves the meibomian glands and points towards the conjunctival surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The meibomian glands lie deep within the tarsal plate, so infection points toward the palpebral conjunctiva rather than the skin surface.

answers.text: Requires systemic antibiotics rather than warm compresses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both types are initially treated with warm compresses four times daily. Systemic antibiotics are not routinely needed for either form.

answers.text: Infects the glands of Zeis at the lash base

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The glands of Zeis and Moll are at the lash base — their infection produces a hordeolum externum (stye), which points toward the skin.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the gland locations: Zeis and Moll glands are at the lash base (externum), while meibomian glands are deep within the tarsus (internum). This determines the direction of pointing.
Exactly. Anatomical localisation determines where the swelling points: meibomian (deep) → conjunctival side; Zeis/Moll (superficial) → skin side.

interactions.label: Which combination of findings indicates that a periorbital infection has breache

params.question: Which combination of findings indicates that a periorbital infection has breached the orbital septum?

answers.text: Lid oedema with normal eye movements and intact vision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These findings describe preseptal cellulitis — infection anterior to the septum. The absence of proptosis, motility restriction, and visual compromise means the septum has not been breached.

answers.text: Proptosis, restricted painful eye movements, and reduced visual acuity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These three danger signs indicate postseptal (orbital) cellulitis. The orbit is a closed bony box, so infection within it causes forward globe displacement, tethered muscles, and optic nerve compromise.

answers.text: Bilateral lid swelling with fever and cervical lymphadenopathy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Systemic signs such as fever and lymphadenopathy may accompany either preseptal or orbital cellulitis. They do not specifically indicate septal breach — the three orbital signs do.

answers.text: Chemosis, epiphora, and lid-margin crusting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lid-margin crusting suggests blepharitis, a chronic surface condition. While chemosis can occur in orbital cellulitis, this combination does not define septal breach.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three danger signs of orbital cellulitis are proptosis, restricted and painful eye movements, and reduced visual acuity or an afferent pupillary defect. Any one of these demands urgent escalation.
Well done. Any single one of these three signs — proptosis, painful restricted eye movements, or reduced vision — mandates IV antibiotics and urgent CT imaging.

interactions.label: In cavernous sinus thrombosis, cranial nerve VI is the first nerve affected beca

params.question: In cavernous sinus thrombosis, cranial nerve VI is the first nerve affected because it:

answers.text: Has the longest intracranial course of all cranial nerves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While CN VI does have a long intracranial course, that explains its vulnerability to raised intracranial pressure — not specifically to cavernous sinus infection.

answers.text: Innervates the lateral rectus, the largest extraocular muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The lateral rectus is not the largest extraocular muscle. CN VI's vulnerability in CST relates to its anatomical position within the sinus, not the muscle it supplies.

answers.text: Runs through the lumen of the cavernous sinus in direct contact with venous blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Unlike cranial nerves III, IV, V₁, and V₂ which travel in the lateral wall, CN VI passes through the lumen itself. Direct contact with infected thrombotic blood makes it uniquely vulnerable.

answers.text: Enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure, closest to the sinus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CN VI enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure, not the inferior. Its vulnerability in CST is due to its intraluminal position within the cavernous sinus.

overallFeedback.feedback: CN VI runs through the lumen of the cavernous sinus, while the other cranial nerves run in its lateral wall. This direct contact with infected blood makes CN VI the first nerve affected.
Precisely. The intraluminal course of CN VI explains why lateral rectus palsy is the earliest sign of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

interactions.label: On imaging, the finding that distinguishes thyroid eye disease from orbital myos

params.question: On imaging, the finding that distinguishes thyroid eye disease from orbital myositis is:

answers.text: Unilateral involvement of only the superior rectus muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thyroid eye disease typically involves multiple muscles bilaterally. Unilateral single-muscle involvement is more suggestive of orbital myositis or other focal pathology.

answers.text: Enlargement of extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendons

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In thyroid eye disease, TRAb-driven glycosaminoglycan deposition enlarges the muscle bellies while the tendons remain normal. In orbital myositis, both bellies and tendons are thickened.

answers.text: Diffuse thickening of the orbital septum with fat stranding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Septal thickening with fat stranding is more characteristic of orbital cellulitis. The hallmark imaging sign of TED relates specifically to the extraocular muscles.

answers.text: Optic nerve sheath enhancement with increased perineural signal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Optic nerve sheath enhancement suggests optic neuritis or meningioma, not thyroid eye disease. The diagnostic imaging finding in TED is muscle belly enlargement with tendon sparing.

overallFeedback.feedback: In thyroid eye disease, the extraocular muscle bellies enlarge but the tendons are characteristically spared. This tendon-sparing pattern on imaging is the key distinguishing feature from orbital myositis.
Correct. The tendon-sparing pattern is pathognomonic for TED on CT or MRI and reliably distinguishes it from orbital myositis where tendons are also involved.

interactions.label: A 5-year-old presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis over two wee

params.question: A 5-year-old presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis over two weeks. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

answers.text: Prescribe oral antibiotics and review in one week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rapidly progressive proptosis in a child over weeks does not fit a simple infection timeline. This tempo and age group raise suspicion of rhabdomyosarcoma, which requires urgent tissue diagnosis, not empirical antibiotics.

answers.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone for presumed thyroid eye disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thyroid eye disease is rare in young children and does not typically present with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis over weeks. This clinical picture demands tissue diagnosis, not empirical immunosuppression.

answers.text: Arrange urgent referral and biopsy to exclude rhabdomyosarcoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest primary orbital malignancy of childhood. Rapidly progressive proptosis over weeks in a child is this diagnosis until proven otherwise — an oncological emergency requiring urgent biopsy.

answers.text: Observe with serial Hertel measurements over three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Observation is appropriate for slow-growing benign lesions such as capillary haemangioma. In a child with proptosis progressing over weeks, a three-month delay risks metastatic spread of a potential rhabdomyosarcoma.

overallFeedback.feedback: Rapidly progressive proptosis in a child means rhabdomyosarcoma until proven otherwise. This is an oncological emergency requiring urgent biopsy, not observation or empirical treatment.
Exactly. Rapidly progressive proptosis in a child is rhabdomyosarcoma until proven otherwise — one of the four red flags demanding same-day referral.
